name: Astragalus

lead: Astragalus root (huangqi) is a staple tonic herb in traditional Chinese medicine, taken for immune support and healthy ageing. People include it in longevity routines hoping that better general health shows up as a fresher, younger look.

Its polysaccharides, astragalosides and isoflavones are reported to modulate immune signalling and inflammation in cell and animal models, and reviews describe immune, antioxidant and metabolic effects. Human trials are few and small, and none has measured appearance. Astragaloside IV is metabolised to cycloastragenol, which is sold separately.

paras: It is used as a tea, powder, tincture or capsule, and is common in longevity and immune-support stacks. It is typically taken daily over long periods, as a general tonic rather than something with a quick visible result.

Wikipedia states the toxic constituents of other Astragalus species were not found in the species used in supplements, though those other species are toxic to livestock. Human adverse-effect data are not well covered, and chemical analyses note product quality and adulteration issues. It is sold as a supplement.

chain: Tonic herb for immunity and vitality
angle.text: Astragalus root is a classic Chinese tonic taken for immunity and vitality, and longevity enthusiasts include it in stacks aimed at ageing well. The idea is better general health, which shows as a healthier, younger look; research is mostly in the lab.

lead: Astragalus, in this entry, refers to the root of Astragalus membranaceus (also Astragalus mongholicus or A. propinquus), known in traditional Chinese medicine as huangqi.[1][2] It is a perennial legume native to temperate Asia, and the root is one of the best-known tonic herbs in Chinese and Mongolian traditional medicine.[1][2][1] It is promoted in the longevity-supplement category as an immune and anti-ageing tonic.

Its main constituents are polysaccharides, saponins such as astragaloside IV, and isoflavones including calycosin and formononetin.[2][3] Reviews describe immune-stimulant, antioxidant, antidiabetic and other activities, mostly from laboratory and animal work.[1][3][4]
Wikipedia reports limited clinical evidence for Astragalus products.[2] No study found in these sources tests astragalus for facial appearance, skin or hair outcomes.

paras: In traditional Chinese medicine the root is used as a tonic, described in a 2014 review as an immune stimulant, tonic, antioxidant, hepatoprotectant, diuretic, antidiabetic, anticancer and expectorant.[1] A review of its polysaccharide fraction describes use to invigorate the spleen and replenish qi.[3] Wikipedia lists it among the fundamental herbs of traditional Mongolian medicine.[2]

The root contains astragaloside IV and other saponins, polysaccharides (Astragalus polysaccharide, APS) and flavonoids.[3][4][2] Reviews of astragaloside IV and of APS report anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects in cell and animal models.[3][4][5] The saponin cycloastragenol, an astragaloside IV derivative, is marketed separately as a telomerase activator.[2] Chemical analyses have found that the composition of commercial Radix Astragali differs by season and from adulterant plants.[6]

Registered human studies are mostly small and in medical conditions: Phase 2 trials in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease (66 and 76 participants),[7][8] a Phase 2/3 trial in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (120),[9] a Phase 2 study of a herbal formula for cancer fatigue (92, completed),[10] and a 24-person study in healthy adults examining muscle function.[11] The sources consulted do not report results from these studies, and none addresses an appearance outcome.

Wikipedia notes that other Astragalus species poison livestock through alkaloids, nitro compounds and accumulated selenium, and that these constituents have not been detected in A. mongholicus used in supplements and traditional preparations.[2] Selenium toxicity was first characterised in livestock grazing selenium-accumulating Astragalus species.[12] The sources consulted do not describe human adverse effects or drug interactions for the root.
